start: The highest excellence is like (that of) water
end: the low place which all men dislike.
context: Water is Taoism's favourite teacher: it nourishes everything, never fights, and settles where nobody else wants to be.
prompt: Where could you be more like water today?

start: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog
context: The Spirit of the Ocean speaks to a river god who thought himself great. A frog at the bottom of a well takes its circle of sky for the whole sky.
prompt: Which well are you looking up from, and how big is the sky beyond it?

start: He who knows other men is discerning
context: Four short contrasts between outer and inner achievement. Self-knowledge and self-mastery come out ahead every time.
prompt: Which kind of strength are you building: over others, or over yourself?

start: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave
end: it is on the empty space (within), that its use depends.
context: Wheels, bowls and rooms are useful because of what is empty in them. Emptiness is not nothing; it is room.
prompt: Where could some emptiness make your life more useful, not less?

start: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly
context: The most famous passage in Taoist literature. Zhuangzi wonders how firm the line really is between who we think we are and what we experience.
prompt: What are you sure about that might be less solid than it seems?

start: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout
context: The source of the saying 'a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step'. A li is a traditional Chinese measure of distance.
prompt: What is the single step you could take today?

start: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere.
context: The opening line of the last chapter. Polish can be a sign that something is being sold rather than said.
prompt: Whose plain words have you overlooked because they weren't polished?

start: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled
context: Overfilling and oversharpening both defeat their purpose. Knowing when to stop is a skill.
prompt: What are you filling to the brim that would be better left with room?

parts: See how the minnows are darting about!
how can you know that I do not know?
context: Zhuangzi and his friend, the logician Hui Shi, argue on a bridge. Hui Shi asks how anyone can know another creature's joy; Zhuangzi turns the same logic back on him. A playful reminder that strict proof is not the only way we know things, including how others feel.
prompt: Where could you simply enjoy something instead of proving it?

start: The partial becomes complete
context: A string of paradoxes: what bends survives, what is emptied gets filled. Wanting less is a way of receiving more.
prompt: What in your life is 'crooked' now and might yet become straight?

start: Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)?
context: Stirring muddy water only clouds it more. Left alone, the sediment settles by itself.
prompt: What might become clear if you simply stopped stirring it?

parts: When I first began to cut up bullocks
And now I work with my mind and not with my eye.
context: Prince Hui's cook has used the same knife for nineteen years because he follows the natural gaps instead of forcing his way. Mastery means working with the grain.
prompt: Where are you hacking at something that has a natural opening?

start: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water
end: no one is able to carry it out in practice.
context: Water wears down stone. Everyone knows that softness can win, says Laozi, yet hardly anyone lives by it.
prompt: Where could softness achieve what force has not?

start: To know and yet (think) we do not know
context: An echo of Socrates, a world away: the wise hold their knowledge lightly; the sick mind is the one that is sure.
prompt: What do you think you know that you might not?

start: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition
context: Discontent, says Laozi, is the deepest misfortune. Knowing when you have enough is a lasting wealth.
prompt: What would be enough for you, really?

start: He who devotes himself to learning
context: Learning adds; the Tao subtracts. Some growth comes from doing less, not more.
prompt: What could you take away from your days rather than add?

start: A man," replied Confucius, "does not seek
context: Zhuangzi puts these words in the mouth of Confucius. We can only see ourselves clearly in water that is still.
prompt: How could you become still enough to see yourself clearly?

start: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful
end: what the want of skill is.
context: Every idea of 'good' quietly creates its opposite. Labels divide the world as much as they describe it.
prompt: Which label you use creates the very thing you dislike?

start: All things alike go through their processes of activity
context: Everything grows, flourishes and returns to its root, like plants through the seasons. Stillness is the return, not the absence of life.
prompt: What root do you need to return to?

start: The softest thing in the world dashes against
context: What is soft finds its way where the hard cannot. Gentleness has its own power.
prompt: Where could you go further by being gentler?

start: It is wood of no quality, and of no use.
context: A carpenter dismisses a huge old tree as worthless. That evening the tree appears in his dream: being 'useless' is what let it grow so old.
prompt: What 'useless' thing in your life is actually keeping you whole?

start: He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak
context: Often quoted as 'those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know'. Deep understanding tends to be quiet.
prompt: What do you understand best, and how little do you need to say about it?

context: Small knowledge sees a part and takes it for everything. Great knowledge keeps the whole in view.
prompt: What part of a situation have you been mistaking for the whole?

start: But I have three precious things
end: shrinking from taking precedence of others.
context: Laozi's three treasures: gentleness, frugality, and not needing to be first.
prompt: Which of the three treasures could you practise today?

start: Man at his birth is supple and weak
context: Living things bend; dead things are rigid. Flexibility is a sign of life, in bodies and in minds.
prompt: Where have you grown rigid, and how could you soften?

start: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit.
context: Zhuangzi's warning against trying to know everything. A finite life spent chasing the infinite runs out.
prompt: What are you trying to master that could never be finished?

start: The farther that one goes out (from himself), the less he knows.
context: Laozi's paradox for a restless age: understanding is not always found by going further.
prompt: What could you understand by staying where you are?

parts: When she died, I could not help being affected by her death.
passing from one phase to another like the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
context: When Zhuangzi's wife dies, his friend finds him singing and drumming on a bowl. He grieved, he explains, and then saw her death as part of nature's turning seasons.
prompt: Which ending in your life could you see as a change of season?

start: The more that he expends for others
end: the more does he possess of his own
context: Generosity, says Laozi, does not empty us. What we give away somehow enlarges what we have.
prompt: What could you give today that would leave you richer?

start: For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror.
context: A mirror reflects whatever comes and holds onto nothing. Zhuangzi offers it as a picture of a free mind.
prompt: What are you still holding that you could simply let pass through?

start: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust
context: A hunchback and a one-legged man are looking at old tombs when sores suddenly break out on their elbows. Asked if he loathes this, one says no: life is only a loan, and life and death follow each other like day and night.
prompt: If your life is a loan, what are you doing with it?

start: people in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success
context: Many projects fail at the very end, through carelessness when success is near. Laozi asks for the same care at the end as at the beginning.
prompt: What nearly finished thing deserves your full care now?

start: The mushroom of a morning knows not
context: Every creature measures the world by its own lifespan. Zhuangzi invites us to imagine much longer and shorter scales than our own.
prompt: How would today's worry look on the scale of a hundred years?

start: The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps
end: can be found fault with or blamed
context: True skill is so natural that it leaves no marks of effort.
prompt: What do you do so naturally that nobody sees the effort?
